sections.causes_of_post_polio_syndrome: As per research the exact cause of Post Polio Syndrome is unknown. The major cause that is noticed is stress on the motor neurons as a result of post polio infection, that we have already read earlier. After recovering from Polio Infection, gradual nerve degeneration still continues in some Post Polio Virus patients. sections.risk_factors_of_post_polio_syndrome:
There are some factors that can increase the risk of spreading post polio syndrome, which includes the following factors: 

 Age of Initial Illness – If you had Polio Virus infection in adult age rather in childhood your chances of developing Post Polio Syndrome increases. 
 Severity of Polio Virus Infection – More the severity of Polio Virus Infection more the chances of developing Post Polio Syndrome. 
 Unrestricted Physical Activity – Regularly pushing yourself to the limit when exercising could overstress already-stressed motor neurons and raise your risk of developing post-polio syndrome. 
 Recovery – The more quick your recovery after Polio Virus Infection, the less the chances of developing Post Polio Syndrome.

 Joint Pain

sections.diagnosis_of_post_polio_syndrome:
Physicians do not utilise a single diagnostic method to identify PPS. Initially, a physical examination will be performed by a doctor to evaluate your reflexes, sensitivity, and muscular strength. If you have:, they might continue with imaging and further tests. The Doctor will analyse polio infection history, muscular weakness and atrophy, and other potential PPS symptoms for at least a year. Your physician will probably wish to rule out any other potential reasons for your symptoms, such as: 

 Acute Injury 
 Recent Surgery 
 A general lack of exercise because of other factors 
 Exclude skeletal anomalies and neurological disorders 

 To assist in the diagnosis of PPS, a physician may employ any of the following tests: 

 MRI 
 CT Scan 
 Spine Fluid Analysis 
 Muscle Biopsy 
 Electrophysiological Study
sections.complications_of_post_polio_syndrome:
This condition is hardly ever life-threatening but drastic muscle weakness may lead to some complications, which are mentioned as below: 

 Fatigue – This is a very common complication of Post Polio Syndrome. Fatigue may lead to disability even after mild activity. It might also result in issues with focus and memory. 
 Falls – It is easy for you to get out of your balance and fall if your leg muscles are weak. After that, you may fracture a bone, like your hip, which could cause further issues. 
 Pain – Chronic pain can result from musculoskeletal disorders and muscular weakness. 
 Malnutrition – If the nerves and muscles helping chewing and swallowing get involved then it may lead to Malnutrition. 
 Chronic Respiratory Failure – It becomes more difficult to cough and take deep breaths when you have weak diaphragm and chest muscles, which can lead to a buildup of mucus and fluid in your lungs. This may further lead to Chronic Respiratory Failure. 
 Osteoporosis – Osteoporosis and bone density loss are frequently associated with prolonged immobility and inactivity, affecting both genders equally. You should discuss bone density screening with your physician if you have post-polio syndrome.
sections.ayurvedic_overview_of_post_polio_syndrom:
Polio Infection is a Viral infection caused by a virus of the family Picornaviridae. There is no direct correlation of Polio Virus in Ayurveda but can be correlated to Baal Pakshaghata and it may include various Vataj Conditions which we can consider as Post Polio Syndrome. Following are various conditions that may be considered as Post Polio Syndrome: 

 Khanja – This is one of the 80 Vata Vyadhis explained by Acharya Charak. An exacerbated vata becomes trapped in the waist, affecting the tendon tissue of one lower leg and resulting in function loss. We refer to this illness as Khanja. Here, the person limps because they are unable to walk normally. 
 Pangta – This is also one of the 80 Vata Vyadhis explained by Acharya Charaka. Acharya Charaka did not describe this condition more significantly but its brief overview is mentioned by Acharya Sushruta. Pangu is the name for vitiated vayu, which is located in the kati region and causes weakness and flaccidity in the muscles of both lower limbs. In order to shed light on this matter, Acharya Dalhana states that “sarvatha gatighatat pangurityarthah” means the patient’s two legs are weak, making it impossible for them to walk or stand. 
 Pakshaghata – Morbid Vata occupies half of the body, snatching up the siras and snayus and causing looseness in nearly every joint on the affected side. As a result, the patient is unable to perform any function with those specific limbs. Certain patients may experience unconsciousness or semi consciousness. From the face to the lower limbs, the left half of the body is affected by vitiated Vata, we call it Pakshaghata. The condition is known as Ekanga Vata if only one leg is impacted. Sarvangroga is the term for the illness that develops if all four limbs become affected and nonfunctional. 
 Avabahuka – In this condition Vayu vitiated Amsa Pradesh (Vital Point located in the upper back at the junction of neck and shoulder on the either vertebral sides. It blocks the siras (blood vessels) and snayus (ligaments) at that point which causes the shoulder joint to slightly drag or constrict. 
 Above are some conditions that can be considered as Post Polio Syndrome, below we will discuss what Ayurvedic Remedies can help in managing these conditions and improve the quality of life of the patient.
